title: Quality and pertinence of the project's research and innovation objectives (and the extent to which they are ambitious, and go beyond the state of the art)
content:
## 1.1 Quality and pertinence of the R&I objectives; going beyond the state of the art

### Scientific problem and its pertinence to the call

Irrigation decisions for row crops must be made under two compounding and qualitatively distinct layers of uncertainty. The first is epistemic: the true field state — how much water is stored in the root zone and how severely the crop is already water-stressed — is only partially and noisily observable from the ensemble of ground sensors, satellite imagery, and meteorological products that are practically accessible to a research installation or farm. Inference from this incomplete multi-sensor observation is inherently uncertain, and most deployed systems suppress that uncertainty in favour of a point estimate that conflates the model's confidence with its correctness. The second layer is aleatory: even if the current field state were perfectly known, the consequences of each irrigation decision depend on future weather that has not yet occurred, and that weather introduces irreducible variability into any yield or water-use projection. Together, these two layers mean that an irrigation decision-support framework that is epistemically honest must do three things that current systems do poorly in combination: (i) infer the latent field state from multiple uncertain data streams and report that inference as a calibrated probability distribution rather than a point estimate; (ii) simulate how the crop would respond to alternative irrigation decisions under multiple plausible realisations of future weather; and (iii) recommend the irrigation decision that best achieves an agronomic criterion — in this project, water-use efficiency — under the joint distribution of field-state and weather uncertainty, without suppressing that joint distribution at the interface between the diagnostic and prognostic components of the framework.

This project addresses all three components within a single end-to-end framework, applied to a scientifically motivated choice of crop (tomato, RQ1, operator-confirmed) on Hungarian farms accessed via the associated partner AgroVIR. The crop choice has two independent justifications. Physiologically, tomato is strongly responsive to irrigation management: both water deficit and water excess induce distinct and economically significant stress responses in fruit set, fruit quality, and canopy physiology, which makes tomato an especially demanding testbed for a framework that must resolve fine-grained water-stress states from satellite and sensor data. Scientifically, tomato is the crop on which the fellow's doctoral expertise was developed — Dr. Rositsa Cholakova's PhD thesis (summa cum laude, 2020, doi:10.2139/ssrn.5492527) addressed the non-destructive evaluation of the physiological status of drought-stressed tomato plants — which means the ground-truth measurement protocol (the validation component of the project, addressed in OBJ-3) is grounded in demonstrated rather than claimed expertise. This connection between the fellow's doctoral training and the project's validation task is elaborated in sub-section 1.4.

The call HORIZON-MSCA-2026-PF-01 requires fellowships that provide excellent researchers undertaking international mobility (scope requirement SR-01). Both defining features are satisfied: Dr. Rositsa Cholakova is a confirmed experienced researcher undertaking an intra-EU European Fellowship from Plovdiv, Bulgaria to Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, Hungary. The research domain — uncertainty-aware multi-sensor crop water stress diagnosis and water-use-efficient irrigation decision support — addresses European agricultural water-use efficiency and food security, and the project directly serves the call's expected outcome EO-07 (stronger R&I capacity and output among participating organisations; better transfer of knowledge) through the genuine, scientifically necessary exchange of plant-physiology expertise (fellow to host) and geoinformatics and remote-sensing competence (host to fellow). The two-way transfer of knowledge, because it is scientifically required for the project's execution rather than formally arranged, is the mechanism by which EO-07 is served at the level of the individual fellowship.

### Going beyond the state of the art

The state-of-the-art analysis underlying this proposal is grounded in a systematic survey of the literature on multi-sensor crop water stress monitoring. The analysis charts the density of published work across two gradients that together define the scientific frontier: depth of sensor integration, spanning from single-sensor studies at the simpler end to multi-modal fusion studies at the more demanding end; and operational complexity of the target task, spanning from stress detection through to stress quantification, optimisation, and real-time irrigation decision support. Study density falls sharply as both gradients increase simultaneously, and they meet in a single substantially empty region: real-time irrigation decision support integrating high-spatial-resolution PlanetScope imagery within a broader multi-sensor ensemble. This region — the research-gap cell — is the territory the present project occupies.

The novelty claim is designed to be narrow and must be read as such by the evaluator. The proposal does not assert that Earth observation for irrigation is novel — that literature stretches back decades and is well-populated. Nor does it assert that probabilistic modelling for agricultural applications is underdeveloped in general. What the systematic review identifies as genuinely underdeveloped is the end-to-end coupling of three specific capabilities that existing works address separately or in limited pairings:

(i) Learned probabilistic fusion of multi-source Earth observation — Sentinel-1 SAR radar backscatter, Sentinel-2 optical surface reflectance, and secured PlanetScope high-resolution imagery (access confirmed via the Planet platform and API, RQ8) — together with ERA5 meteorological reanalysis and available field observations, into a calibrated posterior distribution over the latent field state;

(ii) Explicit, honest probabilistic estimation of that latent field state (root-zone soil moisture and crop water status, RQ3, operator-confirmed), in which the full posterior distribution is carried forward to the decision stage rather than collapsed to a point estimate at the crop-model interface; and

(iii) Uncertainty-aware irrigation decision optimisation via uncertainty-retaining calibration of the FAO AquaCrop crop model, counterfactual simulation over weather ensembles, and scoring of candidate decisions by expected water-use efficiency (WUE, RQ6, operator-confirmed) under the joint uncertainty from field-state diagnosis and future weather.

Genuine probabilistic precedents exist in the literature and are explicitly acknowledged in the state-of-the-art analysis rather than suppressed in favour of an overreaching novelty claim. Bayesian Maximum Entropy approaches have been applied to multi-source drought indicator fusion; copula-based frameworks link drought indices to irrigation scheduling decisions; dynamic Bayesian network models have been used for latent field-state tracking; and multi-modal fusion network architectures address multi-sensor data integration at the feature level. Each of these works advances one of the three components identified above. None couples all three end-to-end, with uncertainty propagated honestly from the observation layer through the crop-model calibration and into the scored irrigation recommendation. That specific end-to-end coupling, across a multi-source satellite stack that includes confirmed access to PlanetScope at 3 m spatial resolution, is the project's defensible contribution.

The ambition of the claim is calibrated to what can be achieved and validated in a 24-month European Fellowship. The project is framed explicitly as a research prototype at TRL 3–4 (RQ10, operator-confirmed). TRL 3–4 — proof of concept demonstrated in controlled or relevant environment — is the appropriate ambition level for this duration and instrument type. Claiming operational readiness within 24 months would misrepresent what a single-researcher fellowship can deliver, and would also undermine the epistemic honesty that is the project's defining methodological commitment: a framework that overstates its own maturity is inconsistent with a framework that is designed to quantify and report uncertainty honestly. The TRL target is therefore both proportionate and principled.

The methodological architecture that implements the novelty claim operates through a two-route diagnostic design (Routes A and B) that feeds a shared prognostic decision engine, with the full detail of this design addressed in sub-section 1.2. The design is risk-managed by construction: Route B, the homogeneous patch proxy (RQ2, operator-confirmed), is the primary implementation path, while Route A, direct one-step probabilistic fusion, serves as a rigorous alternative implemented for comparison and fallback. Both routes produce the same output form — a posterior distribution over the target field state — and feed the same downstream decision engine, so the project is not existentially dependent on the success of any single architectural assumption.

### The five R&I objectives: quality, measurability, and achievability

The project is structured around five operator-confirmed objectives, each mapped to one or more work packages and associated deliverables. Canonical work package titles and deliverable titles are reproduced exactly as they appear in the canonical reference pack. Due months are stated where confirmed in the canonical reference pack.

---

**Objective OBJ-1 — Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the latent field state**

This objective develops and calibrates the diagnostic component of the end-to-end framework: a probabilistic method that fuses multi-source Earth observation data — Sentinel-1 SAR radar backscatter, Sentinel-2 optical surface reflectance, and secured PlanetScope high-resolution imagery (RQ8) — with ERA5 meteorological reanalysis and field observations into estimates of the latent field state (root-zone soil moisture and crop water status, RQ3) expressed as a calibrated posterior distribution with explicit, honest uncertainty (posterior or prediction intervals) rather than a point estimate. The primary implementation path is Route B — the homogeneous patch proxy (RQ2, operator-confirmed) — within a methodological architecture that also implements Route A (direct probabilistic fusion) as a rigorous comparison baseline and methodological fallback. The full architectural rationale is addressed in sub-section 1.2.

*Measurability and verifiability.* The measurable target, confirmed in the canonical reference pack, is uncertainty-calibrated field-state estimation. The verifiable criterion is that the posterior or prediction intervals produced by the diagnostic model are well-calibrated: specifically, 90% prediction intervals must contain the measured ground-truth value approximately 90% of the time on the validation set (the uncertainty-calibration criterion, RQ5). No fabricated accuracy percentage is asserted as a numerical target, because the project's methodological commitment is calibration fidelity — the correspondence between reported uncertainty and actual coverage — rather than point-estimate precision, and asserting a specific accuracy figure would misrepresent the calibration objective. The formal test of Route B's central structural assumption (RQ9: a co-located seasonal measurement campaign demonstrating statistical covariation between the proxy patch and the target tomato crop) constitutes a second independently verifiable criterion for this objective's methodological foundation.

*Realistic achievability.* OBJ-1 is achievable within the 24-month fellowship for four reasons. First, all required data streams are confirmed and immediately accessible: Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 open Copernicus data; PlanetScope access secured via the Planet platform and API (RQ8); ERA5 meteorological reanalysis from ECMWF; and field observations from Hungarian tomato farms accessed via AgroVIR. Second, the two-route design means the objective is not existentially dependent on any single architectural assumption: if Route B's patch-covariation assumption fails the RQ9 test, Route A provides the fallback without requiring a redesign of the downstream decision engine. Third, the host group at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest — Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics — supplies the multi-sensor EO processing infrastructure, hyperspectral imaging and field spectroscopy facilities, and supervision expertise in remote sensing and multisensor-drone fusion (headed by Dr. András Jung, Head of the Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group, project ELTE TKP2021-NVA-29) that the diagnostic branch requires. Fourth, probabilistic model families capable of returning calibrated posterior distributions over latent variables from noisy multi-sensor inputs — including Bayesian hierarchical models and Gaussian processes — are established and well-supported in scientific computing environments, reducing implementation risk.

*Work package and deliverable.* OBJ-1 is addressed in WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state). The primary deliverable is D1-01 (Diagnostic model specification and calibration report, due month 14).

---

**Objective OBJ-2 — Uncertainty-aware decision engine for water-use-efficient irrigation choice**

This objective develops the prognostic decision component of the framework: uncertainty-aware calibration of the FAO AquaCrop crop model that retains a posterior distribution over model parameters rather than collapsing to a single maximum-likelihood parameter set; counterfactual irrigation simulation over weather ensembles, generating a distribution of simulated crop-water outcomes for each candidate irrigation decision under joint field-state and weather uncertainty; and scoring of candidate decisions by expected water-use efficiency under that joint distribution, with the uncertainty of the recommendation reported alongside it. The decision objective is water-use efficiency (WUE, RQ6, operator-confirmed). The decision engine explicitly propagates uncertainty from OBJ-1's diagnostic branch through to the irrigation recommendation — it is the prognostic half of the honest uncertainty chain that is the project's defining methodological commitment.

*Measurability and verifiability.* The measurable target, confirmed in the canonical reference pack, is an integrated decision engine that scores candidate irrigation decisions by WUE under combined weather and model uncertainty, propagating uncertainty from diagnosis into the recommendation. This is verifiable by inspection: the decision engine must accept the posterior field-state estimate from OBJ-1 as input, run counterfactual simulations over weather ensembles, and return an uncertainty-weighted recommendation score rather than a point recommendation. The quality of the propagated uncertainty is assessed through the same RQ5 calibration criterion that applies to OBJ-1 and OBJ-3, applied end-to-end across the full pipeline.

*Realistic achievability.* OBJ-2 is achievable because it is downstream of OBJ-1 along the project's confirmed critical path: Task T1-03 (calibrate diagnostic branch and produce field-state posterior estimates) produces the calibrated posterior that is the direct input to Task T2-01 (implement uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration), as identified in the project's dependency map. The FAO AquaCrop model is an established, openly available, and well-documented crop simulation model with an active user and development community, reducing integration risk. The uncertainty-aware calibration approach — retaining a parameter posterior consistent with observed data rather than returning a single best-fit parameter set — is a known and tractable class of Bayesian model calibration problem, and its application to AquaCrop is architecturally analogous to established uncertainty-aware crop-model calibration methods in the scientific literature.

*Work package and deliverable.* OBJ-2 is addressed in WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration). The primary deliverable is D2-01 (Decision engine and demonstrator software, due month 20).

---

**Objective OBJ-3 — Field validation and honest uncertainty calibration**

This objective designs and executes the project's field validation protocol on Hungarian tomato farms accessed via AgroVIR, establishing whether the diagnostic and decision components of the framework are credible against independently collected ground truth, and whether the framework's reported uncertainty is well-calibrated in the frequentist sense. The validation protocol is defined before data collection begins. All four of its components are operator-confirmed:

*Ground-truth collection (RQ4).* Non-destructive physiological measurements are collected on Hungarian tomato plants at AgroVIR field sites: chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy and leaf temperature, and spectral reflectance. These four measurement types directly characterise the crop's physiological water-stress status and are the grounding of the fellow's doctoral expertise. A coherence caveat is recorded transparently: these measurements validate the crop-water-status component of the target field state (RQ3) directly, and the root-zone soil-moisture component only indirectly through the plant's water-relations response to soil moisture deficit. This is a methodological transparency note, not a gap; the indirect pathway is mediated by well-understood plant hydraulics, and no additional soil-moisture sensor programme is fabricated beyond the multi-sensor fusion architecture of WP1.

*Uncertainty calibration criterion (RQ5).* 90% prediction intervals produced by the diagnostic branch must contain the measured ground-truth value approximately 90% of the time on the validation set. This frequentist coverage criterion is the necessary condition for the model's reported uncertainty to be meaningful — a model whose 90% intervals cover the true value only 60% of the time is overconfident, and irrigation recommendations based on its apparent precision are epistemically unjustified.

*Pilot success criterion (RQ7).* Pilot success is pre-defined as the RQ5 calibration target being met on the holdout validation set — the dataset of field measurements not used in model calibration. This is the project's go/no-go criterion, specified before data collection so that it cannot be selected post-hoc to produce a favourable outcome.

*Patch covariation test (RQ9).* Route B's structural assumption — that the homogeneous proxy patch genuinely covaries with the target tomato crop at seasonal scale in water-stress signatures — is verified by a co-located seasonal measurement campaign in which the target crop and the proxy patch are measured simultaneously and their water-status signatures are shown to covary statistically. Without this demonstration, Route B's inference chain lacks an empirical foundation and cannot be defended.

*Measurability and verifiability.* All four components are measurable against pre-specified, operator-confirmed criteria. The RQ5 coverage criterion is computable from the validation dataset. The RQ7 pilot-success criterion is a binary judgment against the RQ5 criterion on the holdout set. The RQ9 covariation test is a statistical test of association between the seasonal time series measured on the proxy patch and on the target crop. No additional validation numbers are asserted beyond these four operator-confirmed criteria.

*Realistic achievability.* OBJ-3 is achievable because: the ground-truth measurement protocol (RQ4) falls directly within the fellow's established doctoral expertise in non-destructive crop-stress phenotyping, as elaborated in sub-section 1.4; AgroVIR's confirmed role as associated partner provides access to Hungarian tomato farms as validation sites throughout the growing season; the calibration criterion (RQ5) and pilot-success definition (RQ7) are pre-specified and testable with standard statistical tools; and the patch-covariation campaign (RQ9) is a co-located seasonal measurement exercise that is resource-proportionate to the fellowship duration, running from month 8 through month 24 to cover at least one full growing season.

*Work package and deliverable.* OBJ-3 is addressed in WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration). The primary deliverable is D3-01 (Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report, due month 24).

---

**Objective OBJ-4 — Standalone research demonstrator (web MVP)**

This objective integrates the diagnostic branch produced by OBJ-1 and the decision engine produced by OBJ-2 into a standalone research demonstrator — a working end-to-end pipeline from multi-sensor observation to uncertainty-weighted irrigation recommendation — presented as a web-based research prototype at TRL 3–4 (RQ10, operator-confirmed). The demonstrator is explicitly a research artefact, designed to show that the end-to-end pipeline is technically operable and that uncertainty-weighted recommendations can be presented to a researcher or prospective end user; it is not an operational product, a commercial tool, or a decision-ready advisory service.

*Measurability and verifiability.* The measurable target, confirmed in the canonical reference pack, is a working end-to-end demonstrator that exercises the full observation-to-decision pipeline. At TRL 3–4, verifiability is functional and binary: does the demonstrator accept multi-sensor inputs, run the diagnostic branch, pass its calibrated output to the decision engine, and return an uncertainty-weighted irrigation recommendation with its associated uncertainty range? This is the appropriate verification criterion for proof of concept at this TRL level.

*Realistic achievability.* OBJ-4 is achievable within the 24-month fellowship as an integration deliverable: its two component systems (the diagnostic branch from OBJ-1 and the decision engine from OBJ-2) are developed in WP1 and WP2 respectively, and the integration work (Task T2-03: Build and integrate research demonstrator web MVP) is a sub-task of WP2 that assembles independently validated components into a demonstrable pipeline. The deliberate choice of TRL 3–4 as the target (RQ10) bounds the integration scope to what can be realised in a single-researcher fellowship: a research-level interface sufficient to demonstrate the pipeline's operability and to enable researcher interaction with the uncertainty-weighted recommendations, rather than a deployment-ready product requiring extensive hardening, user testing, and operational integration. The ELTE host group provides the research computing environment in which the demonstrator is built and operated.

*Work package and deliverable.* OBJ-4 is addressed in WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration), specifically through Task T2-03. The primary deliverable is D2-01 (Decision engine and demonstrator software, due month 20).

---

**Objective OBJ-5 — Advancement of the fellow's competences and career**

This objective is the researcher-development component of the MSCA-PF instrument: enhancing Dr. Rositsa Cholakova's scientific, technical, and transferable competences and career perspectives through the fellowship's training, supervision, and two-way transfer of knowledge, as elaborated in sub-sections 1.3 and 1.4. OBJ-5 is distinct from OBJ-1 through OBJ-4 in that its achievable target is defined collaboratively between supervisor and fellow rather than pre-specified unilaterally in the proposal, as the MSCA-PF instrument requires (scope requirement SR-04).

The measurable target, as confirmed in the canonical reference pack, encompasses: a Career Development Plan prepared jointly by Dr. András Jung (supervisor) and Dr. Rositsa Cholakova (fellow) and submitted as a project deliverable at the start of the action, then reviewed and updated during the fellowship; structured transferable-skills training covering the MSCA-PF mandatory dimensions specified in scope requirement SR-03 — digital and AI skills including the responsible use of generative AI in remote-sensing and crop-water modelling and scientific coding; knowledge valorisation; innovation and entrepreneurship; research integrity; and open science/FAIR data stewardship; peer-reviewed publication and conference dissemination of the project's results; and two-way transfer of knowledge evidenced by methods exchange between the fellow and the host group. Specific quantitative targets — publication counts, training hours, thesis co-supervision commitments, seminar counts — are deliberately not asserted in this sub-section, as none were operator-provided and as the Career Development Plan process is the correct instrument for setting them jointly, proportionally, and collaboratively.

*Measurability and verifiability.* OBJ-5 is verifiable through the deliverable structure: the Career Development Plan (D4-01) is a mandatory start-of-action deliverable that records the agreed targets; its review and update at intervals during the fellowship provides a longitudinal record of progress. Training activities, publications, and knowledge-exchange events are recorded in the CDP and its updates throughout the 24-month European Fellowship.

*Realistic achievability.* OBJ-5 is achievable because: the Career Development Plan mechanism is a standard MSCA-PF instrument structure for which the host Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, as a higher education establishment with experience in hosting internationally mobile researchers, has established procedures; the two-way transfer of knowledge is genuinely mutual and scientifically necessary (the fellow's plant-physiology and non-destructive stress-phenotyping expertise is required for OBJ-3; the host's geoinformatics and remote-sensing methods and infrastructure are required for OBJ-1), as detailed in sub-section 1.3; and the transferable-skills dimensions specified in SR-03 are embedded in the project's own scientific practice — probabilistic machine learning, Bayesian model calibration, open-science validation protocol design, and responsible use of AI tools in agricultural modelling — rather than appended as a separate training programme with no scientific connection to the research work plan. Dr. András Jung's track record as a researcher who translated spectroscopic research methods from academic prototype to commercial hardware (co-founder of Cubert GmbH and Brightic Research), combined with his dual habilitations in Computer Science and Crop Sciences, provides the supervision breadth that the knowledge-valorisation and innovation/entrepreneurship training dimension requires.

*Work packages and deliverables.* OBJ-5 is addressed primarily in WP4 (Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge), with dissemination and open-science activities supported by WP5 (Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management). The primary deliverable is D4-01 (Career Development Plan, due month 3). Open-science and dissemination outputs are formalised in D5-01 (Data Management Plan, due month 6) and D5-02 (Dissemination and exploitation plan, due month 6).

---

### Alignment of objectives, outcomes, and call expectations

The five objectives collectively serve expected outcome EO-07 — stronger R&I capacity and output among participating organisations; better transfer of knowledge — through the project's five primary scientific and training outputs: Probabilistic multi-sensor field-state diagnosis method (OUT-1, linked to OBJ-1); Uncertainty-aware AquaCrop decision engine (OUT-2, linked to OBJ-2); Field-validation dataset and uncertainty-calibration evidence (OUT-3, linked to OBJ-3); Standalone research demonstrator (web MVP) (OUT-4, linked to OBJ-4); and Enhanced researcher competences and career readiness (OUT-6, linked to OBJ-5). Objectives OBJ-1 through OBJ-4 are measurable against pre-specified, operator-confirmed, frequentist criteria (RQ5, RQ7, RQ9, TRL 3–4) that cannot be selected post-hoc to produce a favourable appearance of success. OBJ-5 is measurable through the Career Development Plan structure mandated by the instrument. The five objectives are ambitious — the end-to-end probabilistic coupling they implement occupies the substantially empty cell of the systematic literature review's research-gap matrix — and honest: the TRL 3–4 target, the explicit RQ3/RQ4 coherence caveat, and the two-route fallback design are all deliberate transparency commitments rather than hedges.
